item.title: Modeling couplings and quench dynamics of hundred-qubit quantum processors
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Continuous unitary transformations derive effective Hamiltonians in under 1 hour per design point on one GPU for a 96-transmon array with 60 couplers. Coupled with semiclassical Monte Carlo, they model quench dynamics of 100 qubits and 180 couplers at half filling (1029-dimensional sector).

Grade 0.402 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Simon Pettersson Fors, Eric Djäknegren, Jorge Fernández-Pendás, Anton Frisk Kockum

Figure

Effective-model quench dynamics for a 280-transmon array (100 qubits, 180 couplers). Plots display time evolution of sublattice occupations, spreading of excitation clusters, and crossover from ballistic to diffusive transport under staggered detuning.

Asks

Which multi-qubit coherent imperfections and dynamical observables in hundred-qubit processors can be predicted classically at the device level?

But

Captures relaxation, thermalization, local densities, and low-order correlators, but fails to predict individual bitstring probabilities for cross-entropy benchmarks. Truncation limits direct diagonalization to detunings exceeding anharmonicity.

Tools

continuous unitary transformations (flow equations) · sign generator for bosonic models · discrete truncated Wigner approximation (DTWA) · excitation-cluster expansion (LCE)

Abstract

Quantum processors now operate beyond the reach of exact classical simulation, yet their design and verification rest on precise models of the device. Understanding which properties of quantum processors can still be predicted on classical computers is central both to building these machines and to delimiting claims of quantum advantage. Here we address this question at the device level, using continuous unitary transformations to derive effective Hamiltonians non-perturbatively for two-dimensional superconducting processors at a cost polynomial in qubit number. For a 96-transmon array with tunable couplers, we extract the effective qubit couplings, state-dependent interactions (e.g., ZZ couplings), and eigenstate locality that guide processor design. This computation parallelizes over tensor contractions and thus takes an hour at most per design point on a single GPU, enabling rapid design iterations of the full array. Combining these effective models with semiclassical sampling, we then predict the quench dynamics of 100 qubits and 180 couplers at half filling, a sector of dimension 10²⁹, and validate the approach against exact dynamics of smaller arrays. We show that our approach captures relaxation, thermalization, and transport, but not the bitstring statistics underlying cross-entropy benchmarks. The predicted transport carries a fingerprint of the device: under a staggered detuning, excitations cross over from ballistic to diffusive spreading, slow down at a doublon resonance, and diffuse at different rates on each sublattice. Our results chart which observables lie within classical reach and offer a practical tool for designing future devices.

item.title: Characterizing a neutral atom quantum simulator accessible in cloud
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Effective noisy open-system model fitted to cloud-accessible input-output data captures dynamics of the Fresnel neutral-atom simulator, identifying quasi-static detuning and SPAM errors as leading noise sources.

Grade 0.385 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Andrea Muratori, Francesco Minardi, Tommaso Calarco, Felix Motzoi

Figure

Measured average Rydberg excitation probability versus pulse duration t compared to the optimized effective noise model for datasets dyn_0 and dyn_1.

Asks

Can an effective dynamical noise model of a cloud-accessible neutral-atom quantum simulator be reconstructed solely from remote input-output measurements?

But

Inferable parameters are effective rather than microscopic; constrained by limited observability through cloud interface with global controls only.

Tools

Pasqal Fresnel quantum simulator · open-system Lindblad master equation · Bayesian parameter estimation · numerical optimization

Abstract

Quantum simulators have become a reality in recent years, with several platforms now remotely accessible through the cloud. These systems give researchers the opportunity to run quantum programs without requiring either a dedicated laboratory or extensive experimental expertise, and, in several cases, they have already enabled the execution of relevant protocols with remarkable results. However, despite the impressive progress in the performance of these machines, they still suffer from various noise sources, some of which are not always completely clear to the end user, which limits their applicability to tasks that are sufficiently robust against noise of various kinds. In this work, we investigate the behavior of Fresnel, a remotely accessible neutral-atom analog quantum simulator provided by Pasqal. We design and perform a series of experiments probing the machine's response to various pulse sequences and experimental settings, and identify the main noise sources affecting its dynamics. Based on these data, we construct an effective model of the system's noisy evolution and use numerical optimization to infer the noise strengths. The resulting model accurately reproduces the simulator's dynamics, showing how effective noise models can be built for cloud-based quantum resources.

item.title: End-to-End Quantum Algorithm for Differential Equations: Application to Simulating a Biomolecular System
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — End-to-end quantum solver for the linearized Poisson-Boltzmann equation achieves total quantum gate cost polylogarithmic in grid points Ng and quasilinear in 1/ε, matching classical preprocessing cost in polylog⁡(Ng,1/ε).

Grade 0.377 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Mohsen Bagherimehrab, Daniyaal Farooqi, Gavin K. Brennen, Barry C. Sanders, Alán Aspuru-Guzik

Figure

Normalized computational cost scaling versus spatial grid points Ng and target accuracy 1/ε, contrasting polylogarithmic quantum gate cost against classical geometric multigrid scaling.

Asks

Can an end-to-end quantum algorithm solve a practical variable-coefficient partial differential equation with rigorous gate costs, classical inputs, and classical outputs without relying on abstract oracles?

But

Treats algorithmic estimation error ε independently of spatial discretization error; applies to linearized regime with bounded variable coefficients.

Tools

diagonal wavelet preconditioning · block encoding via multiscale refinement · quantum linear system algorithms · fixed-point amplitude amplification · quantum phase estimation

Abstract

Quantum algorithms for differential equations have the potential for substantial algorithmic speedups over classical methods. However, they rely on certain assumptions and abstract oracle specifications that leave their practical feasibility and computational advantages for realistic applications unclear. Here we formalize the concept of an end-to-end quantum algorithm for differential equations as one that accepts classical inputs and returns classical outputs, and provide implementations for algorithmic primitives in constructing such algorithms. We present a tailored end-to-end quantum algorithm for the linearized Poisson-Boltzmann (LPB) equation, a partial differential equation (PDE) with variable coefficients widely used in simulating a biomolecular system. We explicitly implement all aspects of the algorithm, from preparing an initial state to generating a quantum solution and estimating properties of the system. In particular, we develop a new discrete representation for variable-coefficient PDEs on a grid that enables efficient implementation of the operator oracle, and build on a recent technique based on optimal wavelet preconditioning to generate a quantum solution with a cost independent of the condition number of the discretized operator. We show the algorithm can be implemented by quantum circuits of size polylogarithmic in both the number of grid points N_g and the inverse of the desired accuracy ε, with an overall gate cost polylogarithmic in N_g and quasilinear in 1/ε. We also show the classical preprocessing to construct the circuits has polylogarithmic cost in N_g and 1/ε. Our work provides a concrete end-to-end quantum algorithm for a PDE of practical value, demonstrates an exponential improvement in scaling with N_g over classical methods, and provides a foundation for assessing its potential quantum advantage in practice.

item.title: All Non-Contextual Pauli Hamiltonians are Free-Fermion in Disguise
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Every non-contextual Pauli Hamiltonian is twin-free-fermion-disguised and carries a Jordan-Wigner-like fermion-to-qubit encoding.

Grade 0.364 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Theory of Trotter Error with Commutator Scaling” · Andrew M. Projansky, Weishi Wang, Kevin A. Reiss, James D. Whitfield

Figure

Euler diagram showing the containment hierarchy of solvable Pauli Hamiltonian classes, placing non-contextual Hamiltonians (HNC) strictly inside twin-free-fermion-disguised Hamiltonians (HFFD).

Asks

What is the structural and computational relationship between non-contextual Pauli Hamiltonians and free-fermion solvable models?

Before

Non-contextual Hamiltonians were known to interpolate between commuting and anticommuting sectors with diagonalizing unitaries computable in polynomial time (Patel, Yen, and Izmaylov 2023), but their containment within free-fermion-disguised classes was unproved.

But

Non-contextual and twin-free-fermion-disguised ground states remain NP-hard to find, and worst-case Trotter-free Hamiltonian simulation can still scale exponentially with qubit count.

Tools

Lean proof assistant · frustration graphs and line-graph recognition · Majorana and Dirac operator algebras · twin-free-fermion disguise reductions

Abstract

Decomposing Hamiltonians into classically tractable fragments is central to quantum simulation. One such way of doing so is the contextual subspace decomposition, which expresses the Hamiltonian with respect to non-contextual sets of Paulis. The conditions for contextuality rely on the anticommutation and commutation of Pauli operators; it is therefore natural to make an explicit connection between non-contextuality and fermionic physics. Theoretical work is centered around two theorems: in the first, we consider non-contextual Pauli Hamiltonians and show that they are free-fermion-disguised. In the second we write these Pauli non-contextual Hamiltonians in terms of Majorana and Dirac fermionic operators, showing that they carry a Jordan--Wigner-like fermion-to-qubit encoding. These two central theorems are formalized in the proof assistant language Lean. We use this to describe the space of fermionic non-contextual Hamiltonians, and highlight their relation to the more general class of free-fermion-disguised Hamiltonians. We further develop a heuristic algorithm to find line-graph based free-fermion fragments and their connected components of molecular Hamiltonians. We benchmark our algorithms against non-contextual searches for encoded molecular Hamiltonians and find comparable performance in identifying free-fermion solvable components. Our work has implications for what fragments to consider as useful for quantum simulation.

item.title: Scalable Simulation of Strongly Correlated Fermions with Neural Gaussian Tensor Networks
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Exact amplitude evaluation for 2D fermionic projected entangled-pair states with O(N3/2) cost via local Gaussian parametrization. Direct transfer of 16×16 trained parameters to a 32×32 Hubbard lattice reaches a variational energy per site of −0.758727(33)t.

Grade 0.358 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum simulations with ultracold quantum gases” · Runze Chi, Ao Chen, Garnet Kin-Lic Chan

Figure

Execution time per amplitude plotted against lattice size N=L2. Shows FP32 Gaussian PEPS scaling as O(N3/2), outperforming dense determinant/Pfaffian O(N3) evaluation by an order of magnitude at 64×64 sites.

Asks

Can neural-network wavefunctions achieve scalable, compact representations of strongly correlated 2D fermions without the O(N2) parameter scaling of backflow or the exponential exact-contraction cost of tensor networks?

Before

SCALE gave −0.7501t, SCALE+GFMC gave −0.7548t, and extrapolated MR-nVAFQMC gave −0.7581(17)t on the 32×32 lattice.

But

Evaluated on 2D periodic Hubbard lattices at U/t=8 and 1/8 hole doping; requires fixed delay slot capacities in GPU Pfaffian elimination.

Tools

neural-network Gaussian projected entangled-pair states (NN-GPEPS) · nested-dissection Pfaffian elimination · variational Monte Carlo · convolutional neural networks

Abstract

Accurate simulations of strongly correlated electrons remain a central challenge in computational physics. We introduce neural-network Gaussian projected entangled-pair states (NN-GPEPS), which exploit the locally-entangled subspace of Gaussian states to give an architecture more compatible with modern neural networks and an exact contraction cost of O(N^(3/2)) on two-dimensional lattices. For the Hubbard model at U/t=8 and 1/8 hole doping, we obtain state-of-the-art variational energies in large lattices of up to 1024 sites. These results demonstrate an accurate approach to strongly correlated fermions by connecting neural networks with Gaussian tensor networks.

item.title: A measurement-free quantum error correction protocol for superconducting cavities
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Simulated measurement-free QEC using a three-cavity binomial code corrects single-photon loss with 99% fidelity and achieves logical lifetime gain of G=1.20 to 1.84 over the unprotected Fock encoding.

Grade 0.345 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Q. Rumman Rahman, S. M. Girvin, D. K. Weiss

Figure

QEC gain G(τ) as a function of inter-cycle waiting time τ/T1cav for T1cav=0.5,1,2ms, peaking above 1.0 (break-even) across all tested cavity lifetimes, and single-round infidelity error budgets.

Asks

Can a measurement-free error-correction protocol for photonic modes be adapted to a three-cavity circuit QED platform to surpass break-even without syndrome measurement or feed-forward?

Before

Six-mode photonic architecture using the Chuang-Leung-Yamamoto code (Krastanov et al. 2021); here reduced to three cavities via the lowest-order binomial code.

But

Numerical simulations with sub-5 µs gate sequence; transmon coherence fixed at T1tr=T2tr=300μs; cavity lifetimes between 0.5ms and 2ms.

Tools

three superconducting microwave cavities · Josephson-junction nonlinear couplers · auxiliary transmons · GRAPE pulse optimization

Abstract

The realization of large-scale quantum computation will require quantum error correction (QEC). One way to reduce the demands placed on QEC is to correct dominant physical errors at a lower level before passing the remaining errors to an outer code. Recently, Krastanov et al. [Nat. Commun. 12, 191 (2021)] proposed a measurement-free error-correction protocol based on coherent control of photonic modes that corrects for photon loss. Here, we adapt this approach to a circuit quantum electrodynamics (cQED) architecture using three superconducting microwave cavities coupled by Josephson-junction-based nonlinear elements. We encode the logical qubit in the lowest-order binomial code of one cavity, while the two other cavities serve as ancillas. Using numerical simulations with experimentally realistic parameters, we demonstrate that our protocol can correct single-photon loss with 99% fidelity. Furthermore, we optimize the waiting time between successive rounds of error-correction, and show that the logical lifetime can be extended by a factor of 1.2-1.8 relative to the unprotected Fock |0⟩, |1⟩ encoding, surpassing break-even performance. Our work highlights the potential of gate-based, measurement-free QEC for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

Furthermore, we optimize the waiting time between successive rounds of error-correction, and show that the logical lifetime can be extended by a factor of 1.2-1.8 relative to the unprotected Fock |0⟩, |1⟩ encoding, surpassing break-even performance. Our work highlights the potential of gate-based, measurement-free QEC for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

item.title: Certified Discovery of Quantum Phase Diagrams
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Polynomial-time quantum algorithm and quasipolynomial-time classical algorithm provably map the phase diagram of any smooth geometrically local Hamiltonian family H(x), providing verifiable certificates for continuous transitions without requiring prior symmetry breaking patterns or order parameters.

Grade 0.344 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Practical quantum advantage in quantum simulation” · Yuanxi Liu, John Preskill, Hsin-Yuan Huang

Figure

Schematic of certified phase discovery showing quasi-adiabatic transport from reference states, energy tests pruning failed preparations, and boundary detection via frequency-filtered Hamiltonian gradient probes.

Asks

Can a machine provably discover new quantum phases of matter given only a local Hamiltonian family and unverified reference ground states?

But

Transitions must not be dark (minimum finite-size spectral gap cannot close faster than inverse-polynomially in system size n); requires at least one successful unverified reference state per gapped region.

Tools

quasi-adiabatic transport · frequency-filtered Hamiltonian gradient probe · band-restricted spectral weight · gentle measurement

Abstract

Can a machine provably discover new quantum phases of matter? We show that the answer is yes under physically motivated assumptions. For any smooth family of geometrically local Hamiltonians, we construct an efficient quantum algorithm that outputs the phase diagram to prescribed accuracy and provides a verifiable certificate for every transition it reports. The algorithm takes as input only a classical description of the family together with unverified preparations of reference ground states; no order parameter, symmetry-breaking pattern, or training data are supplied. It succeeds provided that at least one preparation is correct in each gapped region of parameter space. The algorithm explores parameter space by quasi-adiabatically or adiabatically transporting each reference state, detecting the approach of a phase boundary by tapping the transported state with a frequency-filtered local probe: excitations created by the probe witness the closing of the energy gap. We prove that the gap closing for continuous phase transitions can always be detected using the frequency-filtered gradient of the Hamiltonian. The gap-detecting measurement is gentle, so when the ground state is unique a single reusable copy of each reference ground state supports the full exploration (for degenerate ground states, polynomially many copies suffice). The quantum algorithm runs in polynomial time at inverse-polynomial gap resolution. We also give a classical algorithm that runs in quasipolynomial time at constant gap resolution. Numerical experiments demonstrate how our algorithm accurately determines the phase structure of several model quantum systems.
